Sema cites Responsa Rosh, klal 86, that where a person holds one debt through a power of attorney and there is proof he received payment from the borrower, he may still say, "That payment was for another debt owed to me personally," even if he lacks an ordinary migo. Since he can return the authorized note to its owner, it is treated as though already returned, and he can say the money he received was for his own claim. Rosh's reasoning invokes the principle "if you remain silent," as in Bava Kamma concerning property sold to three people at once. If the holder could restructure the situation by returning the note, the law can treat matters as though that step had already occurred. According to Shulchan Aruch below in siman 119, seif 5, following Rambam and Rashba, we do not always apply this "if you remain silent" mechanism at the conclusion of the sugya. Knesset HaGedolah therefore suggests that this ruling of Rosh depends on the dispute there, and perhaps this is why Mechaber omitted the responsum. However, as I explain below in siman 119, even the authorities who reject the principle there may agree in a case like this. The situation there has special features not present here. More fundamentally, Rosh may not need the "if you remain silent" device at all. The usual reason a creditor needs a migo to say "set-off against another debt" is the presumption that a person does not leave a loan secured by a note unpaid while instead paying an oral debt. But that presumption is strong only where both obligations are owed to the same creditor. If one note belongs to one person and the other debt belongs personally to the authorized agent, the borrower may prefer to pay the agent's personal oral debt first. One creditor may be easier for him to deal with while the other is harder. Everyday experience confirms that people choose which creditor to pay based on circumstances rather than simply preferring written over oral debt. Accordingly, where the payment was made to an authorized agent who also has his own independent claim against the borrower, his assertion that the payment was for his personal debt can stand even without a classic migo. The ordinary presumption favoring payment of the written debt does not apply with the same force across two different creditors. Therefore, Rosh's ruling is correct even according to those who limit the "if you remain silent" principle. The agent may say that the payment was for his own debt, and the authorized document remains unaffected.
He has thereby been established as one who made a false claim. Baal HaTerumot cites two views whether the borrower must nevertheless take a hesset oath. One view requires it; the other holds that once the claimant has been established as a false claimant, no oath at all is imposed upon the borrower. Gidulei Terumah rules that there is no hesset oath, as we generally rule where the claimant has been established as false. Shach distinguishes this case: although the holder of the note was shown false regarding the note, it can still be true that the borrower owes him money from some other source. Therefore, if the lender makes that separate claim, the borrower must either pay or swear that he owes nothing. In my opinion, if the lender claims an ordinary definite independent debt, this is obvious and cannot be the dispute in Baal HaTerumot. Remove the note entirely. Even if witnesses say explicitly that this particular note was unquestionably paid, that does not prevent the lender from saying, "You owe me another debt; swear and be exempt." What uncertainty would there be? Rather, the doubtful case is where the alleged other claim is of a kind that cannot itself be collected through beit din. For example, the lender says that the money he received was for avak ribbit, which is not recoverable through court, or for a profit-sharing arrangement where the borrower was trusted to say there were no profits. The lender says: "What you gave me was for that avak ribbit, or for profits which, once paid, you cannot reclaim by saying there had been no profit. This note remains unpaid." The borrower responds that the payment was on the note. There is then no independent monetary claim that can generate an oath, because avak ribbit is not judicially collectible and the profit claim is barred by the borrower's agreed credibility. Baal HaTerumot's doubt is whether the lender can nevertheless impose an oath by claiming that the note was not paid and that the money received related to that collateral matter. Gidulei Terumah correctly rules that he cannot. Once the lender has been established as false concerning the note, and there is no independent actionable monetary claim, there is no basis for an oath.
But before one witness, no, and so forth. Shach writes at length that many authorities, including Tosafot and Ramban in his chiddushim to Bava Batra, treat this like the case of R. Abba's ingot: since the claimant cannot deny the single witness and say no payment occurred, his assertion that the payment was for another debt makes him one who is obligated to swear but cannot swear, and therefore he loses. Shach himself notes a difficulty. We rule that the doctrine "obligated to swear and unable to swear" does not apply to a rabbinic oath. Here the oath required to contradict a single witness against a note is only rabbinic. Shach nevertheless argues that there is still no migo, because if the claimant denied receiving the money he would have to take a severe oath while now, by saying the payment was for another debt, he would avoid it. This is not correct. Shach follows the explanation in Shevuot that the reason there is no migo in the case of R. Abba's ingot is that the alternative claim would force him to contradict the witness under oath. Tosafot in Bava Batra reject that explanation. They hold that such a migo can exist despite the oath. The real reason there is no migo is that where Torah law says an uncontradicted single witness is treated like two because the defendant cannot swear, the claim fails against testimony equivalent to two witnesses. Most authorities accept this explanation, as I establish at length in my rules of migo below in siman 82. We likewise rule that one who was hired before one witness may still possess a migo to deny the hiring, even though doing so would require an oath against the witness. Accordingly, where only a rabbinic oath is involved and the doctrine of "unable to swear, must pay" does not apply, a migo can still be used against the single witness. Tosafot and Ramban in their chiddushim must therefore follow the view that even with a rabbinic oath one can apply the corresponding loss where the claimant cannot swear, as Tosafot write in Shevuot and Bava Metzia concerning a Mishnah-level oath. Ramban, however, in his responsum cited by Baal HaTerumot follows his position in Milchamot to Shevuot that a suspected person who cannot take the Mishnah-level oath may nevertheless collect on his note; we do not say that inability to take a rabbinic or Mishnah oath causes loss. According to that view, the migo remains available here. This is our halachah as well: with a Mishnah-level oath we do not apply the rule that inability to swear causes automatic loss, as seen below in siman 82 where a suspected creditor can collect his note. Therefore the law stated here is correct, and Shach's objection has no force.
We do not say, and so forth. If after payment the creditor sues again and one witness testifies, "You already paid him," Shach holds that this is exactly like R. Abba's ingot. The creditor cannot deny the witness and say, "I was never paid," because he admits receiving the money and says only that it was for another debt. He is therefore obligated to swear but cannot swear. Indeed, I found Rashba in Kiddushin 45 writing explicitly concerning the incident of Avimi and the people of Bei Chozae that there is a migo to deny receipt even though Avimi has one witness, because the resulting oath is only a Mishnah-level oath and we do not apply "unable to swear, must pay" to it. Rashba then says that if one is clever, he should pay again before that witness together with another witness and afterward sue with one witness, thereby creating a Torah oath and the rule of inability to swear. However, this is true only according to the opinion that once the note is weakened, it is completely void and even money already seized is removed. Rama rules like Rosh and those who hold that if the creditor has already seized, we do not remove it from him, even if the seizure occurred before witnesses. Under that view, what does it matter that he cannot contradict the single witness? The entire force of "unable to swear" is that an uncontradicted single witness is treated like two. But even if two witnesses testified that he received money without specifying this note, once he already holds the money he can say it was for another debt and we do not remove it. All the more so with one witness. Even according to those who hold the note is completely void, Baal HaTerumot shows that the issue is disputed. He cites proof from Ketubot: where one witness says a ketubah was paid, the Gemara says a clever husband should bring the case into a Torah-oath framework by paying again before that witness together with another witness and then suing. The Gemara asks that perhaps the woman can say she had two ketubot. This means that even after she already received the money, she can say the payment related to another document and there is no Torah oath against her. Baal HaTerumot answers that perhaps this is because she is already in possession and merely seeks to retain what she received; the burden rests on the claimant to prove the payment was not for another debt. Thus even two witnesses may not extract the money from her without proving the particular debt. This also answers Gidulei Terumah's question against Ramban. Ramban says that with one witness against a claim of set-off there is no application of R. Abba's rule because the oath is rabbinic. Gidulei Terumah asks: but the Gemara explicitly says one can transform the case into a Torah oath, and still worries about two ketubot. There is no difficulty. Baal HaTerumot already distinguished between a creditor using a note to extract money and a person who has already been paid and merely retains the money. In the latter case, even two witnesses do not necessarily extract, because the possessor can say the payment related to another debt and require the claimant to prove otherwise.
Nevertheless, I am puzzled by Ramban if his words are read as saying that with one witness and a claim of set-off there is no oath at all. The whole basis for believing the set-off claim is a migo that he could have denied receiving payment. But had he denied, he would have been subject to the Mishnah-level oath. If saying "set-off" removes even that oath, one could always fabricate the set-off claim merely to escape the oath. What sort of migo is that? Therefore, Ramban must agree that an oath remains necessary. His point is only that the oath generated through this migo does not acquire the full legal force of the original Mishnah-level oath for purposes of "unable to swear, must pay." This resembles what Shach writes in siman 296 concerning a deposit documented in writing. A custodian who says, "I returned it," is believed with an oath through a migo that he could have said it was lost through unavoidable circumstances. Although the alternative claim would have required a Torah oath, the oath arising only through the migo is not itself treated as a full Torah oath for purposes of the doctrine of inability to swear. The same applies here. Even according to those who say inability to take a Mishnah-level oath causes loss, that applies to the oath itself established by the Mishnah. Where the oath arises only secondarily because it is needed to support a migo, its force is weaker and the doctrine of inability to swear does not apply. Ramban's sequence is therefore: first, the set-off claim is not governed by the R. Abba rule because the underlying oath against the document is only rabbinic; and even if one holds that inability to take a Mishnah-level oath can cause loss, this particular oath is not the formal Mishnah oath instituted to reassure the opposing party. It is only an oath needed to sustain the migo. Hence it is not strong enough to trigger the rule that inability to swear causes loss. Thus Ramban does require an oath. This is why Tur did not record any exemption from oath here. I consider this clear. Tosafot in Ketubot 85b, s.v. "I weaken it," also support this understanding. They ask why Rav Pappa's statement that a note is weakened matters if one witness already requires an oath, and answer that Rav Pappa was a relative of the holder of the note. One might ask why Tosafot did not raise the same question from the earlier incident where Rav Pappa sat before Rava. The answer can be that there the holder may have claimed set-off; if Rav Pappa had only the force of one witness, the resulting migo-based oath would not necessarily have the ordinary force. But where Rav Pappa is believed like two, or joined by another witness, the set-off claim is weakened until oath. In the later statement, Rav Pappa himself holds that a set-off claim does not weaken the note at all, so Tosafot had to answer that he was a relative. This reading somewhat supports Ramban. Even so, the conceptual reading just given is preferable to saying there is no oath at all. It also fits Rosh's citation of Rabbenu Tam that reversal of an oath can function like destruction of the note. The matter is difficult, but the conclusion remains that Ramban requires an oath, though not one carrying the full "unable to swear" consequence.

urim_vetumim_urim.he:
ובאו אלו והעידו וכו' אפי' יש בשטר נאמנות סתם מכל מקום נגד עדים לא הימנ' אבל אם יש בו נאמנות נגד עדים דעת הסמ"ע וש"ך ורוב מחברים דנאמן לומר סטראי במגו דהיה מכחיש לעדים והיה נאמן אף דה"ל מגו דהעזה להכחיש העדים ומהר"א ששון חולק ועיין תומים מ"ש להצדיק דברי הסמ"ע וסייעתו ואם יש בידו כת"י שכך קיבל לפרעון דעת הסמ"ע אם הימנ' כבי תרי גם כן יש לו מגו והש"ך חולק דאינו נאמן נגד כת"י ונכון אתו:
חוב אחר וכו' אפילו ר"י בן מיגאש דסבירא ליה בסעיף זה דבנתן סתם יכול לומר לשם מתנה קבלתי ואי' לי' מגו מכל מקום מודה דאי מעידים שראו שנתן לשם פרעון לא מצי למימר לפרעון שטר אחר קבלתיו אף שלא שמעו על איזה חוב פרעו כן העל' הש"ך ונכון:
הרי בטל כו' ואם שני עדים מעידים שבפרעון שטר זה נתנם ושני עדים מכחישים ואומרים סטראי דעת פרת מ"א דשטר בחזקתו ואני כתבתי בתומים דליתא והלוה פטור דהממע"ה:
בטל השטר ואם ישנו בידו חוב אחד משל אחר בהרשאה ויש עדים דפרעו נאמן לומר על חוב אחר שהיה חייב לי פרעו ולא אתרע הך שטרא שבידו מאחר כן כתב הרא"ש ועיין תומים דהעליתי דהוא ד"ה ולית ביה מחלוקת כלל:
אי תפס אפילו בעדים ודוקא מטלטלין אבל לא קרקע ועיין לעיל סי' מ"ו סעיף ל"ז ומ"ש בקונטרס התפיסות:
לא מפקינן מיניה ולכך א"י להטיל היסת על הלוה דיאמר היום אשבע ולמחר תתפוס ממני בעדים ויהיה שלך או החזיר לי שטרי ואשבע או לא אשבע הר"ן:
הרי הוחזק כפרן ועיין תומים דאם אומר שעל חוב אחר היה מקבלו וחוב אחר הוא חוב מוחלט יכול להשביעו עכ"פ היסת דאין חייב לו שום חוב אבל אם החוב האחר לא ניתן לגבות בב"ד רק אם גבה גבה והוא המלוה טוען שגבה ומלוה בשטר עדיין בלתי פרוע והלוה אומר שהיה על מלוה בשטר אין כאן שבועה אפילו היסת דהוחזק כפרן והשטר ודאי בטל ושאר תביעה אין בו דררא דממון לחייב היסת:
שהרי לא פרעו בעדים ר"ל שלא נתנו בתורת פרעון רק סתם והרי יכול לומר ניתן ליה:
וס"ל וכו' דלא שכיח דאדם יתן במתנה במקום בהוא חייב לו וראשון יפרע חובו קודם שיתן במתנה ולכך לא חיישינן במתנה:
בפני ע"א כו' לא מבעיא דלא שייך ביה דין דנסכא דר"א דנימא ביה מתוך שאיל"מ דאף דהיה חייב שבועה אלו הכחיש לעד לא היה רק שבועה דרבנן ובמילתא דרבנן לא אמרינן משאיל"מ אלא אפילו שבועת המשנה אין צריך דלא תיקן שבועה רק במכחיש לעד בפרעון ותקנו חז"ל להפיס דעתו של בעה"ב אבל במודה דקיבל הפרעון רק דאומר סטראי לא שייך הפסת דעת ואין כאן שבועת התקנה כ"כ הרמב"ן בבעה"ת שער י"ט והש"ך האריך לחלוק מתוך הפוסקים דדנו בי' דין דנסכא דר"א ועיין בתומים דהעיקר כדברי הרמב"ן ודלא כש"ך והא דפסק הרמב"ן דאין עליו שבועת המשנה כלל דעת הסמ"ע דאיירי בדכתב ליה נאמנות דאם לא כן דעתו לעיל בריש סימן דלעולם חייב שבועה אפי' דלא טען השבע לי והש"ך לשיטתו דס"ל דא"צ שבועה כמו שארי שטרות מוקי ליה בשטר שאין בו נאמנות ונכון הוא דרמב"ן לא הזכיר כלל מענין נאמנות ועיין תומים דהעליתי דצריך שבועה בכל אופן רק אין דנין בו דין משאיל"מ אפי' למ"ד בשבועת המשנה אמרי' גם כן משאיל"מ:
לא אמרינן כו' ואם תבעו לאחר פרעון בע"א דפרעו והוא טוען סטראי עיין תומים דהעליתי לשיטת הרמ"א דהכריע דאין השטר בטל לגמרי פשיטא דלית בי' דין משאלי"מ רק נשבע ונפטר ואפילו לדעת המחבר דבטל לגמרי מכל מקום במחלוקת שנוי' בין רשב"א לבעה"ת אי יש עליו דין משאלי"מ ועיין תומים ודלא כש"ך ע"ש:
urim_vetumim_urim.en:
And these came and testified, etc. Even if the document contains an ordinary clause of trust, that trust does not prevail against witnesses. But if the document contains a clause granting credibility even against witnesses, Sema, Shach, and most authorities hold that the lender is believed to say, "I applied it to another debt," through a migo that he could have contradicted the witnesses and would have been believed. This is so even though contradicting witnesses is a brazen migo. Mahara Sasson disagrees. See Tumim, where I defended Sema and those who agree with him. If the lender has his own handwriting acknowledging that the payment was toward this debt, Sema holds that if the borrower granted him credibility equivalent to two witnesses he still has a migo. Shach disagrees and says he is not believed against his own handwriting, and Shach is correct.
Another debt, etc. Even R' Yosef ibn Migash, who holds in this seif that when money is given without specification the recipient may say, "I accepted it as a gift," because he has a migo, agrees that if witnesses testify that they saw the money given as payment, the lender cannot say, "I accepted it toward a different debt," even if the witnesses did not hear which debt was being paid. Shach concludes this, correctly.
It is thereby void, etc. If two witnesses testify that the payment was toward this document and two others contradict them and say it was toward another debt, Perach Mateh Aharon holds that the document retains its presumptive validity. In Tumim I wrote that this is incorrect. The borrower is exempt because the claimant must produce proof.
The document is void. If the lender also holds another person's debt by power of attorney, and witnesses testify that the borrower paid him, the lender is believed to say that the payment was toward a different debt personally owed to him, and the document later produced by him is not thereby weakened. So writes Rosh. See Tumim, where I concluded that everyone agrees and there is no dispute.
If he seized. Even if he seized in the presence of witnesses. This applies only to movable property, not land. See above in siman 46, seif 37, and what I wrote in the treatise on seizure.
We do not remove it from him. Therefore the lender cannot impose hesset on the borrower. The borrower may say, "If I swear today, tomorrow you may seize from me in front of witnesses and keep it. Either return my document and I will swear, or I will not swear," Ran.
He has been established as a denier. See Tumim. If the lender says he accepted the money toward another debt and that other debt was a fully collectible debt, he may at least impose hesset on the borrower that no such debt existed. But if the alleged other debt was not judicially collectible and was merely a claim where, if collected, the holder could retain it, and the lender says that he collected that debt while the documented loan remains unpaid, whereas the borrower says the payment was on the documented loan, there is no oath, not even hesset. The lender was established as a false claimant, the document is certainly void, and the other asserted claim lacks sufficient monetary basis to impose hesset.
For he did not pay him before witnesses. Meaning that he did not give it expressly as payment, but only without specification, and the lender can therefore say it was given as a gift.
And he holds, etc. Because it is uncommon for a person to make a gift to someone to whom he owes money. One would ordinarily repay his debt before giving a gift. We therefore do not suspect that it was a gift.
In the presence of one witness, etc. Not only does the rule of R' Abba's piece of silver not apply so as to say that because he cannot swear he must pay, since even had he contradicted the witness his oath would only have been rabbinic, and the rule of "because he cannot swear he must pay" does not apply to a rabbinic oath. He does not even require the mishnaic oath. The enactment of an oath was made where the borrower contradicts a witness regarding payment, to appease the claimant. But where the lender admits receiving the payment and merely says, "I applied it to another debt," there is no need to appease the borrower and no special oath was enacted. So writes Ramban in Baal HaTerumos, gate 19. Shach argues at length from poskim who applied the rule of R' Abba's piece of silver. See Tumim, where I concluded that Ramban is primary, unlike Shach. As for Ramban's ruling that there is no mishnaic oath at all, Sema explains that the case contains a clause of trust, because otherwise Ramban holds at the beginning of the siman that the lender must always swear even without a demand. Shach, following his own view that no oath is required absent a demand, explains Ramban as discussing a document without a trust clause. This is correct, because Ramban does not mention trust at all. See Tumim, where I concluded that an oath is nevertheless required in every case, only we do not apply the rule that inability to swear creates payment liability, even according to those who apply that rule to a mishnaic oath.
We do not say, etc. If after payment the borrower sues him and one witness says that payment occurred while the lender says, "I applied it to another debt," see Tumim. I concluded that according to Rama, who rules that the document is not entirely nullified, it is obvious that the rule of inability to swear and therefore pay does not apply. The lender swears and is exempt. Even according to the Mechaber, who treats the document as entirely void, Rashba and Baal HaTerumos dispute whether that rule applies. See Tumim, unlike Shach.

mechaber.he: אמר לו הלוה הלא שטר חוב זה דמי שור שלקחתי ממך הוא ואתה גבית דמי בשרו ואמר לו בעל השטר כן אני גביתי דמיו אבל מחוב אחר שהי' לי אצלך הואיל והודה שדמי השור הוא החוב ומדמיו נפרע בטל השטר אם יש עדים שפרע לו דמי השור ויש מי שכתב שאע"פ שאין עליו עדים שפרע מדמיו ישבע הלוה היסת שפרעו (והעיקר כסברא הראשונה) (אם ידוע שנתן לו קצת הדמים על חוב אחר לא יוכל לומר על האחרים שהם חוב אחר) (מהרי"ק שורש ק"כ):
mechaber.en: He said to him, “This is a poor man who I took from you, and you have raised his flesh and said to him that the husband of the quaint, I have raised his blood, but another debt that I have given to you is the one who has no witness that he does not have any evidence that he is the first of his life.”

baer_hetev.he:
עדים. כת' הסמ"ע זה פשוט דביש לו עדים אפי' לא הוד' שנפרע מהשור השטר בטל כמ"ש בס"ב ולא הל"ל לשון הואיל והוד' רק שלא רצה המחבר לשנות ל' הרמב"ם ע"כ. והש"ך כת' דזה דוחק לפרש כן דהא גם הטור כת' כיון שהוד' והוא הכריע בהדיא דלא כהרמב"ם לכן נרא' לפרש דמיירי שאין העדים מעידים שקיבל דמי השור בתורת פרעון אלא שאומרים שקיבל מהלוקחים בשר השור ולישנא דאם יש עדים שפרע לו כו' הוא לאו דווקא או דנ"ל דאלוקחים קאי ובהכי ניחא נמי מ"ש הט"ו אם יש עדים שפרע לו דמי השור כו' וא"צ לדחוק כמ"ש הסמ"ע והב"ח דדמי השור לאו דוקא עכ"ל:
השור. כ' הסמ"ע דלר"ת והרא"ש דס"ל אפי' אם מעידין סתם שראו שנתן לו מעות אתרע שטרא כמ"ש בהג"ה בסעיף הקודם ולא קרעינן ליה ולא מגבינן ביה ס"ל בדין זה דמוד' שהיו דמי השור דהשטר בטל לגמרי והי"א ס"ל דאפי' אין עדים כלל שנתן לו דמיו אינו נאמן כיון דמעצמו הוד' שקיבל דמי השור ה"ל כמגו במקום חזק' והש"ך חולק עליו וכת' דגם בזה לא מגבינן ביה ולא קרעינן ע"ש (וע' מ"ש הט"ז בזה) ובש"ך הביא תשובת מהר"ם מלובלין סי' קי"ד במי ששלח שלוחו לקבל מעות כו' ע"ש:
ידוע. צל"ע בדין זה שהוא חידוש ולא נמצא כן בשאר פוסקים גם מהרי"ק גופיה לא החליט כן להלכ' רק צירף אותו לטעמים אחרים ע"ש. ש"ך:
baer_hetev.en:
Witnesses. The Sema writes that this is obvious: if there are witnesses, even if the creditor never admitted that he was paid from the proceeds of the ox, the document is void, as stated in seif 2. The Mechaber therefore need not have used the expression 'since he admitted'; he merely did not wish to alter the Rambam's wording. The Shach writes that this is strained, for the Tur also writes 'since he admitted,' although the Tur explicitly rules differently from the Rambam. He therefore explains that the witnesses do not testify that the creditor received the proceeds of the ox as payment of this debt. Rather, they testify only that he received meat or proceeds from the purchasers of the ox. The wording 'if there are witnesses that he paid him' is therefore not exact, or alternatively it refers to the purchasers. This also resolves the wording of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, 'if there are witnesses that he paid him the value of the ox,' without resorting to the Sema and Bach's forced explanation that 'the value of the ox' is not literal. Thus concludes the Shach.
The ox. The Sema writes that according to Rabbenu Tam and the Rosh, who hold that even if witnesses testify generally that they saw the borrower give the creditor money the document is impaired, as stated in the gloss to the preceding seif, so that it is neither torn up nor collected upon, in this case, where the creditor admits that the money was the proceeds of the ox, the document becomes entirely void. The other cited opinion holds that even where there are no witnesses at all to the payment, the creditor is not believed, because by voluntarily admitting that he received the proceeds of the ox he is asserting a migo against an established presumption. The Shach disagrees and writes that here too the document is neither collected upon nor torn up; see there. See also the Taz. The Shach further cites Responsa Maharam of Lublin, siman 114, concerning one who sent an agent to receive money; see there.
known. A shadow in this sentence is that it is renewing and is not found in the rest of the R&D, it did not decide to circulate it for other reasons. “Third:

ל) טור בשם ה"ר יוסף הלוי ושכן מסתבר וכתב בה"ת בשער י"ט דטעמא משום דמסתמא בפרעון אותו שטר נטל' דהכי אורחא דמלתא
